newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil CVRD sale overwhelmed by lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil CVRD sale overwhelmed by lawsuits.

text.p: Michael Christie
Planning Minister Antonio Kandir remained confident Tuesday that Brazil's auction of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) would go ahead despite an overwhelming flurry of law suits.

In Rio de Janeiro, where the sale was due to have begun at 1000 local time/0900 EDT/1300 GMT but was delayed by court injunctions, about 2,000 stone-throwing leftists and students clashed with riot police, turning the city centre into a battle field.

"The minister is still confident the auction will go ahead," said an aide to Kandir, adding that National Development Bank (BNDES) lawyers were managing to successfully appeal injunctions at a faster rate than opponents were having them issued.
"We are just going to have to wait for the end of the day," the aide said.

The BNDES, which runs Brazil's privatization program, has given itself until 1700 local time/1600 EDT/2000 GMT to get the sell-off of 45 percent of voting shares of CVRD America's biggest privatization to date will be delayed for an uncertain amount of time.
By midday, a BNDES spokesman said at least 18 injunctions had been issued and some eight of those had been revoked.
Officials acknowledged that a lawsuit in Sao Paulo, on which government appeals had twice been rejected, was proving the most troublesome.
"Sao Paulo is the only real problem we face," Kandir's aide said.

The privatization of CVRD, the world's largest iron ore exporter, should raise at least $5.0 billion for the government's coffers once completed and thus qualify as the biggest Latin American state sell-off ever.

CVRD's Carajas mine, deep in the Amazon, holds the world's largest iron ore deposit estimated at 18 billion tonnes. The group, which enjoys a rare public sector reputation for efficiency, also mines copper, gold and manganese.

The sale has attracted considerable controversy, with opponents ranging from former presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco to the country's Catholic bishops accusing the government of selling the country out to foreigners for a pittance.
The flurry of lawsuits against the sale, a favourite tactic of privatization foes, came as no surprise.
Nevertheless, it seems to have overwhelmed Brasilia's small army of 120 lawyers who have been flying around the country in four specially hired jets to take on injunctions.
The legal battle was mirrored outside the Rio de Janeiro bolsa where hundreds of demonstrators trying to break through a security cordon fought with police, throwing rocks and cans.
Police retreating towards the exchange fired stun grenades and tear gas into the crowds and called in water cannons.
Authorities said several people were injured before the violence died down at around midday.
Two multinational consortia were in the bidding for the 45 percent stake of CVRD going under the hammer on Tuesday.
One was being led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN and the other by local pulp, cement and metal concern Votorantim and Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd.
